title: Of ill means employed to a good end
paragraphs: There is a remarkable relation and correspondence in the universal government of the works of nature, which makes it quite clear that it is neither accidental nor run by several masters. The diseases and conditions of our bodies show up in much the same way in states and governments: kingdoms and republics are founded, flourish, and decay with age as we do. We are subject to a build-up of humours, useless and dangerous — whether of the good ones (for even those the physicians fear; and since we have nothing stable in us, they say that an over-brisk and vigorous state of health must be reduced by art, lest our nature, unable to rest in any fixed condition and having nowhere higher to climb to improve itself, make too sudden and disorderly a retreat — which is why they prescribe purges and bleeding for wrestlers, to take down that overflowing health), or else of bad humours, which is the usual cause of sickness. States are very often sick from the same kind of repletion, and various sorts of purging have commonly been applied. Sometimes a great mass of families is sent out to clear the country, seeking new homes elsewhere and encroaching on others. In this way our ancient Franks came from the deepest part of Germany to seize Gaul and drive out its first inhabitants; in this way the infinite flood of men who came into Italy under Brennus and others was put together; in this way the Goths and Vandals, and also the people who now hold Greece, left their native country to go settle elsewhere with more room. There are scarcely two or three small corners of the world that have not felt the effects of such migrations. The Romans set up their colonies by this means: seeing their city grow immensely populous, they relieved it of the more superfluous people and sent them to inhabit and cultivate lands they had conquered. Sometimes too they kept wars going on purpose against some of their enemies, not only to keep their own men in action, for fear that idleness, the mother of corruption, might bring some worse trouble on them:
"Et patimur longae pacis mala; saevior armis Luxuria incumbit."
["And we suffer the ills of a long peace; luxury is more pernicious than war." — Juvenal, vi. 291.]

but also to serve as a bloodletting for their republic, to vent a little of the overheated energy of their youth, to prune the branches off a stock too thick with wood. It was for this end that they kept up so long a war with Carthage.

In the Treaty of Brétigny, Edward III of England would not include in the general peace he then made with our king the dispute over the Duchy of Brittany, so that he might have somewhere to discharge his soldiers, and so that the huge number of Englishmen he had brought over to serve him here would not flood back into England. This was also one reason our King Philip agreed to send his son John on a foreign expedition: so that he could take with him a great many of the hot young men then in his pay.

There are many today who talk the same way, wishing this heat among us could be discharged in some neighbouring war, for fear that all the diseased humours currently dominant in this body politic of ours may spread further, keep the fever at its peak, and finally cause our total ruin. And in truth a foreign war is far more bearable than a civil one. But I do not believe God will favour so unjust a design as for us to pick a quarrel with others for our own advantage:
"Nil mihi tam valde placeat, Rhamnusia virgo, Quod temere invitis suscipiatur heris."
["Rhamnusian virgin, let nothing ever so greatly please me which is taken without justice from the unwilling owners" — Catullus, lxviii. 77.]

And yet the weakness of our condition often forces us into the necessity of using bad means to a good end. Lycurgus, the most accomplished lawgiver there ever was, virtuous as he was, invented this very unjust practice of forcing the helots, who were their slaves, to be drunk, so that the Spartans, seeing them so lost and drowned in wine, might come to detest the excess of this vice. And yet those were still more to blame who long ago allowed condemned criminals, whatever their manner of death, to be cut up alive by the physicians, to give a true picture of our inward parts and build their art on firmer evidence. For if we must go to extremes, it is more excusable to do it for the health of the soul than of the body, as the Romans trained their people in valour and contempt for danger and death by those furious spectacles of gladiators and fencers, who, having to fight to the death, cut, mangled, and killed one another in front of them:
"Quid vesani aliud sibi vult ars impia ludi, Quid mortes juvenum, quid sanguine pasta voluptas?"
["What other end does the impious art of the gladiators propose to itself, what the slaughter of young men, what pleasure fed with blood." — Prudentius, Contra Symmachum, ii. 643.]
And this custom carried on until the time of the Emperor Theodosius:

"Arripe dilatam tua, dux, in tempora famam, Quodque patris superest, successor laudis habeto Nullus in urbe cadat, cujus sit poena voluptas.... Jam solis contenta feris, infamis arena Nulla cruentatis homicidia ludat in armis."

["Prince, take the honours delayed for thy reign, and be successor to thy fathers; henceforth let none at Rome be slain for sport. Let beasts' blood stain the infamous arena, and no more homicides be there acted." — Prudentius, Contra Symmachum, ii. 643.]

It was, in truth, an astonishing example, and very useful for training the populace, to see every day before their eyes a hundred, two hundred, even a thousand pairs of armed men cut each other to pieces with such steady courage that they were never heard to utter one syllable of weakness or pity, never seen to turn their backs, nor take so much as a single cowardly step to avoid a blow, but rather offered their necks to their opponent's sword and presented themselves to receive the stroke. Many of them, when mortally wounded, would send to ask the spectators whether they were satisfied with their conduct before they lay down to die on the spot. It was not enough for them to fight and die bravely — they had to do it cheerfully too, so that they were hissed and cursed if they showed any hesitation about receiving their death. The young girls themselves egged them on:
"Consurgit ad ictus, Et, quoties victor ferrum jugulo inserit, illa Delicias ait esse suas, pectusque jacentis Virgo modesta jubet converso pollice rumpi."

["The modest virgin is so delighted with the sport, that she applauds the blow, and when the victor bathes his sword in his fellow's throat, she says it is her pleasure, and with turned thumb orders him to rip up the bosom of the prostrate victim." — Prudentius, Contra Symmachum, ii. 617.]

The early Romans only condemned criminals to this use, but later they employed innocent slaves in the work, and even free men who sold themselves for it; and beyond that senators and Roman knights, and women too:
"Nunc caput in mortem vendunt, et funus arena, Atque hostem sibi quisque parat, cum bella quiescunt."
["They sell themselves to death and the circus, and, since the wars are ceased, each for himself a foe prepares." — Manilius, Astron., iv. 225.]
"Hos inter fremitus novosque lusus.... Stat sexus rudis insciusque ferri, Et pugnas capit improbus viriles;"
["Amidst these tumults and new sports, the tender sex, unskilled in arms, immodestly engaged in manly fights." — Statius, Sylv., i. 6, 51.]

I would find this strange and incredible, if we did not see every day in our own wars many thousands of men from other nations, for money, staking their blood and their lives in quarrels that are no concern of theirs.
